title: Working with the Borrow Checker
intro: The borrow checker is the part of the compiler that enforces ownership, borrowing and mutable borrows. When it says no, the program is usually one small change away from compiling: borrow instead of move, copy a small value out first, split a struct into parts, take a value out with `take`, or keep an index instead of a reference. Each fix has a cost, and some errors point at a design that should change.

coming_from.go: Go lets any pointer write and keeps whatever is reachable alive. The habits that meet a Rust error are a pointer into a slice that `append` then moves, two slices sharing one array, a pointer to the `range` variable (before Go 1.22), and a method that changes a struct while a loop reads another part of it.
coming_from.kotlin: Two names can reach one object and either can change it. `List` is a read-only view, and `MutableList` or a cast gets the writes back. Rust puts "read" or "change" in the signature (`&` or `&mut`) and refuses a second writer.
coming_from.python: `b = a` makes a second name for one list, and either name changes it. That is documented behaviour, not a bug. In Rust two names that both change one list are E0499: one owner changes it and the other borrows it for a call, or you clone.
coming_from.typescript: `const b = a` is a second name for the same array, and either can push. In Rust two names that both change one array are E0499: one owner changes it and the other borrows it for a call, or you clone.
coming_from.java: Two names can reach one object and any of them can change it. A getter that returns the internal `List` lets the caller change it unless you wrap it (`Collections.unmodifiableList`). Rust's `&[T]` getter is read-only, and objects that point at each other become ids, or `Rc` with `Weak`.
coming_from.csharp: A property that returns the internal `List<T>` lets the caller change it, unless it returns an `IReadOnlyList<T>`. Rust's `&[T]` getter is read-only, and a separate `&mut self` method says that the caller may change.
coming_from.c: A `realloc` that moves an array leaves every pointer into it dangling. GCC's `-Wall` warns about a direct use after `realloc`, and says nothing when the `realloc` is inside a `push` helper. Rust refuses the push while a reference into the array is alive.
coming_from.cpp: A moved-from `std::string` or `std::vector` is valid but in an unspecified state (libstdc++ leaves it empty), so `v[0]` on a moved-from vector crashes. A reference into a vector survives a `push_back` until it does not. Rust refuses both at compile time: a moved value cannot be used, and a push cannot happen while a reference is alive.

notes: Read a borrow error as three places: where the value was moved or borrowed, the use that clashes, and a later use that keeps the first alive. A fix moves one of the three.

`self.note(..)` takes `&mut self`, which borrows all of `self`. A field access such as `self.log.push(..)` names one field, and the compiler can see that two fields are separate places. Either use the field, work out what to do first and then call the method, or split the struct.
`clone` is a fix that compiles and costs a copy. It is right for a small value that you need twice, and wrong when two parts of the program must see the same changes.
When an error keeps coming back, change the design: one owner per piece of state, indices or keys instead of references between values, and "decide with `&self`, then apply with `&mut self`".

gotcha.title: A method call while a field is being read
gotcha.looks_fine: In these languages a loop reads one list while a helper method appends to another list of the same object. Nothing is wrong with it.
gotcha.rust_sees: E0502: cannot borrow `*self` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable. The loop borrows `self.items`. `self.note(..)` takes `&mut self`, which borrows the whole of `self`, and `items` is part of it. The compiler checks the call with the signature alone, so it must assume `note` could change `items` while the loop reads it.
gotcha.why: This run is fine because `note` only touches `log`. The compiler reasons from the signature, not the body, and a `note` that also pushed to `items` would change a list while a loop walks it. That is a real bug, and the languages differ in what it does: an exception in Java, Kotlin and C#; in Go the loop never reaches the new items; in Python and TypeScript it visits them, so the loop may never end (removing an item instead makes it skip the next one); undefined behaviour in C and C++. [Mutable borrows](/learn/mutable-borrows/#changing-a-list-while-looping-over-it) has the runs. Name the field (`self.log.push(..)`), work out what to log first and call the method afterwards (as `fixed.rs` does), or split the struct so the log is its own type.

go.says: Go runs this and prints the log. `range` reads the slice once at the start, and `note` appends to a different slice.
go.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints the log. `note` changes `log`, not the list the loop walks, so there is no `ConcurrentModificationException`.
kotlin.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

python.says: Python prints the log. `note` changes `self.log`, not the list being looped over.
python.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

typescript.says: Prints the log. `note` pushes to `log`, not to the array the loop walks.
typescript.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

java.says: Java runs this and prints the log. `note` adds to `log`; the list being iterated is not changed, so no `ConcurrentModificationException`.
java.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

csharp.says: C# runs this and prints the log. `foreach` walks `items`; `Note` changes `Log`, a different list.
csharp.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

c.says: C runs this and prints the log. `note` writes into the `log` array of the same struct; the loop reads `items`. Nothing checks that `note` stays away from `items`.
c.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]

cpp.says: C++ runs this and prints the log. `note` pushes to `log`. If it pushed to `items` the push could reallocate the vector under the loop's iterators, and nothing would say so.
cpp.out: log: ["out of stock: bolt", "out of stock: washer"]
